details: The following tables are a comparison of machine learning software such as software frameworks, libraries, and computer programs used for machine learning.

explainer.lead: A comparison of machine learning software helps people choose among frameworks, libraries, and programs for building machine learning systems. It puts candidate tools side by side so their differences can be judged against the needs of a particular project.

tiers.eli5: Choosing machine learning software is like choosing a bicycle for a trip: the best one depends on where you are going and what you need to carry. A comparison lines up the choices and checks them against the same requirements. This makes it easier to pick a suitable tool instead of guessing.
tiers.practitioner: Use a comparison to narrow down frameworks, libraries, and programs before committing a project to one of them. Define the required task and workflow, compare candidates against the same criteria, and test the leading options on a representative example. A feature checklist alone can miss integration problems or practical differences between tools.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, the comparison is a structured evaluation of a set S of machine learning frameworks, libraries, or programs using a common set of criteria C. It supports software selection for a specified use case, but its conclusions depend on the chosen criteria and test setting rather than establishing one universally best tool.

explainer.example: A team needs software for a small classification project. It compares two frameworks and one library against the same project requirements, then builds the same simple classifier with each candidate and chooses the one that fits its workflow best.

usedIn.name: Model development
usedIn.detail: Helps a project team select software for building and testing machine learning models.

usedIn.name: Research projects
usedIn.detail: Helps researchers identify frameworks or libraries that fit an planned experiment.

usedIn.name: Software planning
usedIn.detail: Provides a common basis for discussing candidate tools before adoption.

explainer.intuition: Machine learning software comes in different forms, including frameworks, libraries, and complete programs. Comparing them with shared criteria turns a vague choice into a decision tied to the work that needs to be done.
howItWorks: Describe the machine learning task and required workflow.
List candidate frameworks, libraries, and programs.
Apply the same comparison criteria to every candidate.
Try the strongest candidates on a representative task.
Choose the option that best fits the requirements.
explainer.whyItMatters: A structured comparison makes software selection clearer and connects the choice to actual project needs. It also gives teams a repeatable way to evaluate several candidates instead of relying on an unstructured impression.
misconceptions: It does not identify one tool that is best for every project.
A framework, a library, and a complete program are not necessarily interchangeable.
A table of features is not the same as testing the software on the intended task.
